```text
Observation Activity
Here’s a great exercise to figure out if you are stuck in the middle of me-
diocre mountain when it comes to your game. It will work best if you take
the time to write out your thoughts and reactions.
   Suppose that someone has been tasked to observe you as you play
your normal game. They are to record everything they see you do – every
action you take – every hand you play, every hand you fold, how you
treat your tablemates, how you respond to 3-bets, etc. Would they see
you multi-tasking or are you very attentive to each hand? Would they see
you engaging in a pre-game routine or just winging it? Be very specific
about what they would see you doing.
   Now for the fun part: imagine that this record of your actions will be
published for all to see and that it will stand as the permanent record of
your play and your playing ability.
   Would you be happy with what’s about to be reported? If not, what
would you change? Be very specific and write out exactly what your ideal
playing session would look like. What “right” things would you want seen
and recorded with regard to your play?
   Also, do this same exercise with your study sessions. What would the
observer see you doing in relation to your preparation? How do you study
to keep up with this ever evolving game? Do you approach it with gusto
or do you procrastinate? Do you go the extra mile or do the bare mini-
mum? Would you be pleased if your typical study session was shown to
the world? If not, what would you change? What types of study habits
would you be proud to have on display?
   When I have clients complete this exercise, most admit that they would
not be proud of what would be revealed. They acknowledge that they are
not working up to their ability – in some cases they are not even close. If
you have a similar reaction, take the time to really plan out what your ideal
```

```text
thing we each need to realize about ourselves is that “every falling away

spise ourselves” (1970). When we fail to live up to our highest potential,
it registers with our unconscious. Likewise, when we do what is good and
worthy that registers, too. It’s like a system of debits and credits. When
you live up to what you are capable of, that’s a deposit that can contrib-
ute to your long-term well-being. Conversely, poor habits such as pro-
crastination count as a debit and can cause long-term negativity and
stress as well as de-motivation.

Defining Your Plans
At this point, we’ve covered a great deal of information about the theo-
retical importance of knowing what you want and committing to a proc-
ess to get it. Let’s move into some concrete steps that you can use to
outline your plans.
    All great achievements start with a definitive description of what you’d
like to accomplish. What is your ideal outcome in poker? For maximum mo-
tivation, it’s important to delineate a vision that is powerfully motivating. As
Baum describes it, “just like small fires create small amounts of heat, weak
desires create weak results” (1999). If you want to transform a small fire
into a raging inferno your goal must inspire you greatly. A small goal is not
the answer. What would you go after if you saw no obstacles in your way?
What is the best outcome you could possibly hope for?
    Over the years I have worked with many poker players, who only held
vague, nebulous, weakly formed goals for their poker career. When I ask
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance

game” or “I’d like to leave my day job and play professionally, someday.”
There have been thousands of studies done on the process of goal setting
and the vast majority show it to be an effective technique for peak per-
formance, but only when it is done in a certain manner. There is not one
study of which I am aware that shows that setting a vague goal elicits op-
timal or maximal results. An effective desire statement needs to be pow-
erful, written in the positive, specific, and measurable. There is nothing
that is as effective as a made up mind. Once you make up your mind
about what you want to achieve and then start directing all of your re-
sources to it, you will be unstoppable.

Activity: Goals Reflection
Studies show that only a small percentage of people take the time to
write out their goals. This is a shame given that we know that having clear
goals increases focus, drive, and motivation. Goals reflect those things
that we would like to achieve. To get a better handle on your goals, take a
bit of time to answer the following questions in as much detail as you can:

     ♠ What are your poker goals? Be as specific and clear as you can be.
     ♠ Why are these goals important to you?
     ♠ Are your poker goals challenging and meaningful to you?
     ♠ What actions will you need to take to achieve them?
     ♠ What means can you use to track your progress towards your
        goals?

Mental Contrasting
Now that you have written out some goals, it’s time to start considering
all the benefits that will come to you when you achieve your deepest de-
sires. There’s no doubt that achieving certain levels of success brings all
sorts of rewards and benefits. Take some time and write out what you
imagine the rewards and benefits to be. In the past, most motivational
gurus would have you stop right here. All that would remain for you to do
```

```text
                                                         What’s Your Why?

is to visualize achieving success along with all the rewards and benefits
you just outlined. We now know that this is not the path to success, and
in fact may even harm your chances of success!
    While it is important to consider all the good things that may happen as
a result of achieving our goals, an even more important thing to do is to
consider all of your potential obstacles. Gabriele Oettingen is the current
leading researcher on motivation, and she has found that simply looking at
the positives often sets us up to fail and is actually very de-motivating!
Let me explain why this is so.
    The process of visualizing all the good things that can come our way is
a blissful experience and it feels very calming and relaxing. That is exactly
the problem, according to Oettingen. She says that “in dreaming it, you
undercut the energy you need to do it” (2014). In fact, in her recent book
Rethinking Positive Thinking (2014) she shares some research that shows
that the blood pressure of people who fantasize about desired outcomes
decreases. Relaxation is certainly a good thing during downtime, but if
you are trying to focus and motivate yourself to work towards a goal, it’s
the last thing you want! Working to reach your goals requires energy.
    Oettingen came up with a unique strategy to help inspire motivation and
increase energy, which she calls mental contrasting. The idea behind mental
contrasting is that you work yourself up into a motivated state by thinking
about the potential obstacles that stand in your way. To be technical, you
feel what she calls a necessity to act. To conjure up this feeling, this neces-
sity to act, you should write out every obstacle you can think of, then size
this list up against your reward–benefit list from earlier so that you can
make plans to tackle them. This is the vital step that most people skip when
they start thinking about outcomes they would like to attain.
    Let me tip you off about another important caveat. For this to work,
you need to believe that you are capable of achieving your goals. This is
known as self-efficacy; without it, thinking about all of your obstacles will
just depress you and your motivation will drop. The trick is to make sure
that your dreams are challenging but feasible.
    The upside of mental contrasting is that while it will mostly energize
```

```text
   Mental contrasting is an essential step on the road to success, but it is

If This Then That: Implementation Intentions
We are getting to the end of our planning time now. You have come up
with a desire that you are committed to achieving and you have gone
through the exercise of mentally contrasting the benefits of your goals
with possible obstacles in order to get fired up. The last piece of the puz-
zle is to come up with plans to attain your goals and there is a specific
strategy for coming up with your plans that will increase the likelihood of
you sticking to them.
    The strategy is called an implementation intention; the researcher who
is most associated with this process is Peter Gollwitzer. According to
Gollwitzer, implementation intentions take the form of thinking, “if situa-
tion X arises, then I’ll do Y in response” and are also known as “if this, then
that” plans (1999). For example, let’s say that I plan to do five hand his-
tory reviews per day. I can rely on willpower and motivation to get them
done by deciding to do them whenever I feel like it, or I can come up with
an implementation intention, which essentially pre-commits me to doing
them. Maybe I will pre-decide that when I have my daily morning coffee, I
will do my five hand history reviews. Or I might decide that I will do them
right after I eat my breakfast. It doesn’t matter what activity I tie the ac-
tivity to as long as it is something I do every day. In this way, I know ex-
actly when I will be taking care of it. There is absolutely no guess work to
it. Also, tying my commitment to a pre-existing habit like coffee drinking
makes it more likely to become habitualized. You can choose to tie your
```

```text
                                                         What’s Your Why?

new routine to any pre-existing habit you already have – coffee drinking

proven method for reducing procrastination, which is a problem for about
98% of the human race.
    Let’s put the steps together so you can start taking committed action
towards your chief poker goals:

   ♠ Step 1. Write out your desire statement. It can be as detailed as
       you like. The more specific it is, the better.
   ♠ Step 2. Write out the rewards and benefits that will likely come
       your way as a result of your achieving your primary aim(s). Some
       rewards are fairly obvious like money and recognition, but there
       are others that may be less obvious like freedom from a boring job
       or the self-actualization that comes from mastery. Try to think of
       as many rewards and benefits as you can.
   ♠ Step 3. List out all potential obstacles and roadblocks. As with the
       benefits and rewards, try to think of as many of these as you can.
       An example of an obstacle is lack of time to devote to study.
       Another might be lack of knowledge about what to study. The key
       is to use this resulting list as a starting point for putting together a
       list of possible solutions. Also, you’ll need to decide if you have
       what it takes to overcome these potential stumbling blocks. If yes,
       go to the next step. If no come up with a new desire statement
       and go through the mental contrasting process again.
   ♠ Step 4. Create an action plan for overcoming said obstacles and
       attaining your goals. For example, if lack of time is a major
       obstacle, you’ll need to decide what you will give up in order to
       make time for study and play. If you are not sure what to study,
       perhaps you need to hire a coach or seek out other training
       resources. The most important thing is to come up with a plan that
       you are committed to taking action on. The next section will
       provide you with even more ideas for creating a solid action plan.
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance

Activity: Creating a Daily Action Plan
While implementation intentions are the cornerstone for achieving our
desires, we would be well advised to write out a comprehensive action
plan that includes all of our planned activities for reaching our goals. Be-
cause we have gone through the above steps, we have a very clear grasp
of our present reality. The only question now is what do we need to do
daily to transform our desires into goal achievement?
    Most poker players function best when they have a concrete written
plan or roadmap of daily activities. Your written plans should include tech-
nical training as well as mental game training. For example, every elite
poker player I know follows some sort of eating and exercise plan in order
to enhance their mental game.
    Let’s say that one of your goals is to study for 10 hours a week. You’ll
want to decide how many days of the week as well as what materials you
will study. If you are new to poker, be aware that there are many great
books you can study. For example, Jonathan Little has written or edited
the definitive guides to tournament play (Secrets of Professional Tour-
nament Poker and Jonathan Little’s Excelling at No-Limit Hold’em). There
are many reputable video training sites you can join, too. Will you seek
outside coaching? How will you evaluate how much you are learning?
How will you track your progress? What will you do if you are short on
time? Can you find small windows of time in which to study? Short
amounts of study each day are more important to long-term improve-
ment than irregular cram sessions.
    A recreational player might set a target of playing 20 hours of $1/$2
No-Limit Hold’Em per month with an eye towards moving up to $2/$5
once their bankroll reaches a certain amount. If you set a goal like this, how
many hours per day (or per week) are you going to devote to playing?
Where are the best games spread? Do they occur at a specific time and
day of the week? When in your day are you the most focused and clear?
Schedule your day in ways that make you most likely to be successful.
    There are many avenues of mental game training that you can include
in your plan. Perhaps you want to start a daily meditation practice or a
```

```text
    As you are making your action plan, I urge you to think about which ac-
tivities are going to be of the highest value to your pursuit. Peak per-
formers cannot afford to waste time, so it’s critical to look for the one
thing or that vital 20% of activities that offer the biggest bang for your
buck. Also, it is critical to revisit your action plans every so often to make
changes and adjustments. Nothing is set in stone and it’s all about finding
what works best for you. Remember, you are running your own race, so
your action plan is specific to you and it doesn’t matter what someone
else would write. Also, keep in mind that this is going to be the focus of
your strategy over the long haul. It’s okay to modify it over time, but
there are no shortcuts for peak performance. Be in it for the long term. If
you take the time to be clear about your priorities and then work dili-
gently towards them, you will improve.

Are You Willing to Pay The Price?
Ben Hogan is considered by many to be one of the greatest golfers of all
time. His willingness to pay the price for greatness was legendary. His
daily practices included hitting over 1,000 balls over a period of six hours.
His playing partner, Jimmy Demaret, wrote about a time when Hogan
shot a record 10 birdies in the opening round of the Rochester Open.
While everyone else went to the clubhouse to drink and celebrate, Hogan
went to the practice tee. When Demaret asked him about it, Hogan said,
“If a man can shoot ten birdies, there’s no reason he can’t shoot eighteen”
(1954). Hogan was a man who understood the price extracted by excel-
lence, and he was clearly willing to pay it.
    No matter what your overall goals and desires are, everything comes
with a price. If you decide to pursue a path of poker excellence, you’ll be
forced to give up other opportunities. There is only so much time in the day
and you’ll have to make some decisions about how you want to spend your
time. Your action plan lays out the exact price you’ll have to pay if you want
to achieve peak performance. Whether or not you will attain peak perform-
```
